subject: Polity
sub_topic: Parliamentary committees — PAC, Estimates, Public Undertakings

concepts.name: Public Accounts Committee (PAC): Composition and Constitutional Basis
key_dimensions: Statutory vs. conventional basis — PAC is NOT constitutionally mandated; it is a Rules of Procedure creation
Composition: 22 members (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha), term of 1 year
UPSC trap: Speaker nominates members, but by convention the Chair is always from the Opposition party (since 1967)
Distinction: PAC examines PAST expenditure (post-facto audit), unlike Estimates Committee which is forward-looking

concepts.name: PAC's Relationship with the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)
key_dimensions: CAG's Audit Reports are the primary input for PAC — PAC cannot function effectively without CAG reports
CAG acts as the 'eyes and ears' or 'friend, philosopher and guide' of PAC
PAC examines Appropriation Accounts and Finance Accounts of the Union Government
Critical distinction: CAG audits, PAC scrutinizes — two separate but interdependent constitutional/statutory roles
UPSC trap: PAC cannot direct the CAG; CAG is independent under Article 148

concepts.name: Scope and Jurisdiction of PAC: What It Can and Cannot Do
key_dimensions: PAC examines whether money was spent as sanctioned by Parliament — legality, regularity, and propriety of expenditure
UPSC trap: PAC is NOT an appellate body — it cannot question policy decisions of the government
PAC cannot interfere with day-to-day administration or question the wisdom behind a policy
PAC's recommendations are NOT binding on the Executive — government can reject them with explanation
Exclusion: Amounts under Secret Service expenditure are exempt from PAC scrutiny

concepts.name: Estimates Committee: Composition, Origin, and Forward-Looking Role
key_dimensions: Largest Parliamentary Financial Committee: 30 members, ALL from Lok Sabha only (Rajya Sabha has NO representation)
UPSC trap: Unlike PAC, Rajya Sabha has NO role in Estimates Committee — this is a critical distinction
Origin: Set up in 1950 on the recommendation of John Mathai; modeled on British Select Committee on Estimates
Examines Budget Estimates BEFORE expenditure — suggests economies, improvements in organization and efficiency
Term: 1 year; members re-eligible; Chair is from the ruling party (unlike PAC where Chair is from Opposition)

concepts.name: Estimates Committee: Powers, Functions, and Limitations
key_dimensions: Can suggest 'alternative policies' to bring about efficiency — broader mandate than PAC
Cannot examine expenditure already incurred — purely prospective/forward-looking
UPSC trap: Estimates Committee reports have NO binding force — executive is NOT obligated to implement them
Cannot examine estimates of Railway Budget separately (historically) — Railways had separate budgeting process
Does NOT examine all estimates every year — selects specific ministries/departments on a rotational basis

concepts.name: Committee on Public Undertakings (CPU): Composition and Dual Mandate
key_dimensions: Composition: 22 members (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha), term of 1 year — mirrors PAC in structure
Created in 1964 based on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee
Hybrid mandate: Combines functions of BOTH PAC (audit scrutiny) and Estimates Committee (efficiency review) for PSUs
Examines reports of CAG on Public Sector Undertakings AND the Estimates relating to PSUs
UPSC trap: CPU examines PSUs — but it CANNOT examine Government companies where Parliament has no financial stake

concepts.name: CPU: Scope, Exclusions, and Limitations
key_dimensions: CPU cannot examine matters of day-to-day administration or matters of major government policy
UPSC trap: CPU cannot examine a PSU if a Committee of Parliament/State Legislature is already examining it
It does NOT examine the Indian Railways, which has a separate parliamentary oversight mechanism
CPU can suggest improvements in working of PSUs but its recommendations are NOT binding
Key limitation: CPU cannot question the policy under which a PSU was established

concepts.name: Comparative Analysis: PAC vs. Estimates Committee vs. CPU
key_dimensions: Time orientation: PAC = retrospective; Estimates = prospective; CPU = both (retrospective audit + prospective efficiency)
Rajya Sabha representation: PAC = Yes (7 members); Estimates = NO; CPU = Yes (7 members)
Subject matter: PAC = all govt expenditure; Estimates = budget estimates of ministries; CPU = PSUs only
UPSC trap: All three committees' recommendations are advisory/non-binding — none can compel the executive
Chair convention: PAC = Opposition leader; Estimates = Ruling party; CPU = typically ruling party

concepts.name: Financial Committees vs. Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs): Overlap and Distinction
key_dimensions: DRSCs (24 committees) examine Demands for Grants of respective Ministries — creating functional overlap with Estimates Committee
DRSCs are joint committees (both Houses); Estimates Committee is Lok Sabha only
UPSC trap: A Ministry's estimates examined by DRSC may NOT be re-examined by Estimates Committee for that year
Financial Committees (PAC, Estimates, CPU) have longer institutional history and specialized financial audit focus
DRSCs introduced in 1993 — significantly reduced the workload and relevance of Estimates Committee

concepts.name: Parliamentary Oversight Mechanism: Financial Accountability Framework
key_dimensions: Constitutional basis for financial accountability: Articles 112–117 (Budget), Article 266 (Consolidated Fund), Article 148 (CAG)
The tripod of financial accountability: Parliament → CAG → Parliamentary Committees
UPSC trap: Financial committees oversee EXECUTIVE spending, NOT legislative or judicial expenditure (charged expenditures are non-votable)
Charged vs. Voted expenditure: PAC can examine both, but voted expenditure is primary focus
Accountability loop: Spending → CAG Audit → PAC/CPU scrutiny → Action Taken Reports by Government

concepts.name: Action Taken Reports (ATRs) and Follow-up Mechanism of Financial Committees
key_dimensions: Ministries must submit ATRs to PAC/CPU explaining action taken on committee recommendations
PAC classifies ATRs into: Accepted, Not accepted (with reasons), Action being taken, Further examination needed
UPSC trap: If a Ministry does NOT submit ATR, the Committee can call the Ministry Secretary — but cannot penalize
Pendency of ATRs is a chronic criticism of the financial committee system in India
Unlike UK's PAC, Indian PAC has NO power to summon Ministers (only civil servants/officials appear)

concepts.name: Privileges and Powers of Parliamentary Financial Committees
key_dimensions: Committees can send for persons, papers, and records — quasi-judicial investigative power
UPSC trap: Ministers do NOT appear before financial committees — only Secretaries and senior officials testify
Committees can take evidence on oath in some cases — strengthens fact-finding capacity
Proceedings of committees are covered by Parliamentary privilege — witnesses have immunity for bona fide testimony
Committees CANNOT summon the President, Vice-President, or judges of Supreme Court/High Courts

concepts.name: PAC and Audit of Autonomous Bodies and Aided Institutions
key_dimensions: CAG's audit extends to bodies substantially funded by the Union Government — PAC can examine these
UPSC trap: Grant-in-aid recipients beyond a threshold come under CAG/PAC purview — not just direct government departments
Controversy: Private companies receiving government grants — extent of PAC scrutiny is debated
PAC examined the 2G spectrum scam, Coalgate, Commonwealth Games irregularities — demonstrating broad real-world reach
PSUs where government holds <51% equity — gray area for CPU examination

concepts.name: Historical Evolution and Reforms in Parliamentary Financial Committees
key_dimensions: PAC established in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) — oldest financial committee
Estimates Committee: Formally constituted in 1950 after independence; existed in rudimentary form earlier
CPU: Established 1964 as PSU sector grew significantly post-independence planning
Key reform demand: Giving PAC prospective powers (like a 'pre-audit' role) — currently rejected to maintain separation
Recommendation to merge PAC and CPU has been periodically raised but not implemented

concepts.name: Procedural Rules Governing Financial Committees: Quorum, Meetings, and Reports
key_dimensions: Quorum: One-third of total membership required for a valid meeting of financial committees
Reports are presented to the full House — they are 'laid on the table' of Lok Sabha (and Rajya Sabha for PAC/CPU)
UPSC trap: Financial committee reports do NOT require voting/approval by the House to be valid — they are advisory documents
Dissent notes can be appended by minority members — but the majority report is the official committee report
Committees can sit during recess of Parliament — their work is continuous, not session-bound

concepts.name: Estimates Committee and Policy Scrutiny: The 'Alternative Policy' Dimension
key_dimensions: Unique power: Estimates Committee CAN suggest 'alternative policies' — goes beyond mere audit into policy territory
UPSC trap: Despite this power, Estimates Committee CANNOT question the policy approved by Parliament itself
This power distinguishes Estimates Committee from PAC (which strictly cannot suggest policy alternatives)
Practical limitation: Suggestions on alternative policies are rarely implemented — executive discretion is paramount
This creates a conceptual tension: oversight body suggesting policy vs. separation of powers principle

concepts.name: Public Accounts Committee: Comparison with UK's PAC
key_dimensions: UK's PAC: Minister cannot appear; same convention in India — but UK PAC has stronger follow-up enforcement culture
India's PAC Chair from Opposition since 1967 — convention, NOT constitutional/statutory requirement (UPSC trap)
UK's National Audit Office (NAO) vs. India's CAG — both serve as the investigative arm of respective PACs
Key difference: UK PAC has more frequent public hearings with higher media visibility; India's PAC is less publicized
India's PAC covers ALL government spending; UK's PAC similarly covers all public expenditure

concepts.name: Interaction Between Financial Committees and Consolidated Fund of India
key_dimensions: Article 266: All revenues received and loans raised by the Government go into the Consolidated Fund
No money can be withdrawn from Consolidated Fund except under Appropriation Act — PAC verifies this compliance
UPSC trap: Contingency Fund (Article 267) withdrawals are also subject to PAC scrutiny post-facto
Public Account of India (Article 266(2)) — transactions here are NOT subject to vote of Parliament; yet CAG/PAC can scrutinize
Financial committees complete the accountability loop for all three accounts: Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, Public Account

concepts.name: Criticism and Weaknesses of India's Parliamentary Financial Committee System
key_dimensions: Systemic weakness: Time lag — PAC examines accounts 2-3 years after expenditure, reducing corrective relevance
Pendency of ATRs means many PAC recommendations remain unimplemented for years
UPSC trap: Committees have NO power to punish non-compliance — accountability is moral/political, not legal
Members lack technical expertise in public finance, auditing, and PSU management — diluting scrutiny quality
Proliferation of DRSCs since 1993 has fragmented financial oversight, creating duplication and reduced focus

concepts.name: Special Situations: Joint Committees of Parliament vs. Financial Committees
key_dimensions: Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs) are ad hoc, issue-specific (e.g., 2G scam JPC) — different from standing financial committees
UPSC trap: JPCs can examine policy questions directly — they are NOT bound by the 'no policy questioning' convention of PAC
Financial committees are STANDING committees (permanent); JPCs are SELECT/AD HOC committees (temporary)
A JPC can have broader powers granted by the specific resolution creating it — more flexible than PAC/CPU
Overlap controversy: When both JPC and PAC examine the same scam, jurisdictional questions arise about primacy
